title: Pearl Divers of the Gulf
summary: How pearl divers of the Arabian Gulf, including the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia, worked the sea for pearls and why the trade came to an end.
poll: Pearl divers had one of the hardest jobs in history.

versions.title: Divers of the Sea
versions.text:
Long ago, men on the Gulf coast dove in the sea. They went to find pearls. Some came from the east of Saudi Arabia.

A pearl is a small, round gem. It grows in a sea animal. The animal is an oyster. It has a hard shell.

Each summer, the boats set out. The sea was warm then. The men stayed out for months.

A diver took one big breath. He put a clip on his nose. He held a stone on a rope. It took him down fast. He got to the sea floor. He put oysters in a bag. Then he tugged the rope. A man on the boat pulled him up. A dive took a minute or two. Each man dove a lot.

Most oysters had no pearl. But a fine one was worth a lot.

Then, things changed. Farms in Japan made pearls. It was a new way. Then oil was found. Men went to work in oil. We still tell tales of the divers.

Long ago, brave men on the Gulf coast dove deep into the sea to hunt for pearls. Some of them came from towns on the east coast of Saudi Arabia.

A pearl is a small, shiny gem. It grows inside a sea animal called an oyster. The oyster lives in a hard shell on the sea floor.

versions.title: Pearl Divers of the Gulf
versions.text:
For hundreds of years, men along the coast of the Arabian Gulf dove deep into the sea to search for pearls. Some of them lived in towns on the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia, such as Darin and Al-Qatif. For these families, pearls were the main source of income.

A natural pearl forms inside an oyster, a sea animal with a hard shell. When something small gets inside the shell, the oyster covers it with layer after layer of a smooth, shiny material. Over several years, these layers grow into a pearl.

Every summer, when the water was warm, wooden boats called dhows sailed out to the oyster beds. A crew of divers, pullers, and a captain stayed at sea for about four months.

A diver took one deep breath and put a clip on his nose. A heavy stone tied to a rope pulled him down quickly. On the sea floor, he filled a basket with oysters. Then he tugged the rope, and a puller on the dhow hauled him up. Each dive lasted a minute or two, and divers went down dozens of times a day.

The next morning, the crew opened the oysters. Most had no pearl, but one perfect pearl could be worth a fortune.

In the 1920s and 1930s, pearl diving began to decline. In Japan, people learned to grow pearls on farms, and these cheaper pearls filled the markets. Then oil was discovered in Saudi Arabia in 1938, and many men left the sea for oil jobs. Today, the divers are remembered as a proud part of Gulf history.

versions.title: Pearl Divers of the Gulf: Treasure from the Deep
versions.text:
For centuries, men along the coast of the Arabian Gulf plunged deep into the sea to search for natural pearls. Some of them lived in towns on the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia, such as Darin and Al-Qatif, and for many of these coastal communities, pearling was the most important livelihood.

A natural pearl forms inside an oyster when an irritant, such as a tiny parasite or a fragment of shell, becomes trapped within its shell. To protect itself, the oyster coats the irritant with layer after layer of nacre, the smooth, shimmering substance that also lines the interior of its shell, and over several years these layers gradually build up into a pearl.

Every summer, when the water was warm enough, wooden dhows sailed out to the oyster beds. Each crew, which included divers, pullers, a cook, and a captain, remained at sea for approximately four months, often encouraged by a singer whose traditional songs set the rhythm of the work.

A diver took one deep breath, closed his nose with a clip, and descended rapidly, dragged by a heavy stone attached to a rope. On the sea floor, he collected oysters in a basket hanging from his neck until his breath ran short. Then he tugged the rope, and a puller on the deck hauled him to the surface. Each dive lasted a minute or two, and divers repeated this exhausting routine dozens of times a day.

The following morning, the crew opened the oysters. Most contained nothing, but a single flawless pearl could be worth a fortune.

During the 1920s and 1930s, the pearling industry declined sharply. Japanese farmers had developed a method for producing cultured pearls by deliberately placing an irritant inside oysters, and these cheaper pearls flooded international markets. Then oil was discovered in Saudi Arabia in 1938, offering steadier employment. Today, pearl diving survives as treasured heritage, celebrated in museums, songs, and festivals.

versions.title: Pearl Divers of the Gulf: Treasure from the Deep
versions.text:
For many successive centuries, men residing along the extended coastline of the Arabian Gulf plunged repeatedly deep into the surrounding sea in persistent search of natural pearls. Some among them inhabited towns situated along the eastern coast of present-day Saudi Arabia, such as Darin and Al-Qatif. For many of these coastal communities, pearling represented by far the most significant available livelihood, simultaneously supporting merchants, boat builders, and entire extended families.

A natural pearl begins forming inside a living oyster at the moment an irritant, such as a microscopic parasite or a tiny fragment of shell, becomes trapped within its protective shell. In order to protect itself, the oyster methodically coats the irritant with layer after layer of nacre, the smooth, iridescent substance that also lines the interior of its own shell. Over the course of several years these accumulating layers gradually coalesce into a single, lustrous pearl.

Each summer, once the surrounding water had grown warm enough, traditional wooden dhows sailed outward toward the known oyster beds. Each crew, which typically included divers, pullers, a cook, and a captain, remained continuously at sea for approximately four demanding months, enduring scorching temperatures and extremely cramped conditions, frequently encouraged by a professional singer whose traditional melodies set the working rhythm of their physically demanding labor.

A diver would inhale a single deep breath, close his nostrils firmly with a small clip, and descend rapidly, dragged downward by a heavy stone attached to a length of rope. Upon reaching the sea floor, he collected available oysters within a basket suspended from his neck until his held breath inevitably ran short. Afterward, he would tug sharply on the rope, signaling a waiting puller stationed on deck to haul him back to the surface. Each dive lasted only a minute or two. Divers repeated this exhausting routine dozens of times throughout each day, despite considerable dangers from jellyfish, sharp coral, and painful ear injuries.

The following morning, the crew would methodically open the accumulated oysters one by one, and although the overwhelming majority contained nothing whatsoever of value, a single flawless pearl could nevertheless prove worth an extraordinary fortune to its finder.

During the 1920s and 1930s, the traditional pearling industry declined with remarkable rapidity. Japanese entrepreneurs had successfully perfected a technique for producing cultured pearls by deliberately inserting an artificial irritant inside farmed oysters, and these considerably less expensive cultured pearls subsequently flooded international markets precisely when a worldwide economic depression was reducing overall demand for luxury goods. Subsequently, petroleum was discovered within Saudi Arabia in 1938, offering former divers considerably more dependable employment. Today, traditional pearl diving survives primarily as treasured cultural heritage, commemorated in museums, traditional songs, and regional festivals held throughout the area.

versions.title: Pearl Divers of the Gulf: Treasure from the Deep
versions.text:
For many successive centuries, men residing along the extended coastline of the Arabian Gulf plunged repeatedly and perilously deep into the surrounding sea in persistent, lifelong search of natural pearls. Some among them inhabited towns situated along the eastern coast of present-day Saudi Arabia, such as Darin and Al-Qatif, and for many of these coastal communities, pearling represented by far the most economically significant available livelihood, simultaneously supporting merchants, boat builders, rope makers, and entire extended families across successive generations.

A natural pearl begins forming inside a living oyster at the precise biological moment an irritant, such as a microscopic parasite or a minuscule fragment of shell, becomes accidentally trapped within its protective shell cavity. In order to protect itself from this unwelcome foreign intrusion, the oyster methodically coats the irritant with successive layer upon layer of nacre, the smooth, iridescent organic substance that also lines the interior surface of its own shell, and over the course of several patient years these gradually accumulating concentric layers eventually coalesce into a single, lustrous pearl of genuine value.

Each summer, once the surrounding Gulf waters had grown sufficiently warm, traditional wooden dhows sailed outward toward the known and carefully guarded oyster beds. Each crew, which typically included numerous divers, their corresponding pullers, a dedicated cook, and an experienced captain, remained continuously at sea for approximately four demanding months, enduring scorching ambient temperatures and extremely cramped onboard conditions throughout, frequently encouraged and sustained by a professional singer whose traditional melodies established the working rhythm of their physically exhausting and dangerous labor.

A diver would inhale a single deep breath, close his nostrils firmly with a specialized clip, and descend rapidly beneath the surface, dragged downward by a heavy stone attached securely to a length of rope. Upon reaching the sea floor, he collected available oysters within a woven basket suspended from his neck until his held breath inevitably and urgently ran short. Afterward, he would tug sharply and deliberately on the rope, signaling a waiting puller stationed on deck above to haul him swiftly back to the surface and breathable air. Each individual dive lasted only a minute or two at most, and divers repeated this exhausting, physically punishing routine dozens of separate times throughout each working day, despite facing considerable and well-documented dangers from venomous jellyfish, sharp coral formations, and painful ear injuries sustained through repeated and rapid pressure changes.

The following morning, the assembled crew would methodically open the accumulated oysters one by one in careful sequence, and although the overwhelming majority contained nothing whatsoever of commercial value, a single flawless pearl could nevertheless prove worth an extraordinary fortune to the fortunate crew that discovered it.

During the 1920s and 1930s, the traditional pearling industry declined with remarkable and ultimately devastating economic rapidity. Japanese entrepreneurs had successfully perfected a reliable commercial technique for producing cultured pearls by deliberately inserting an artificial irritant inside carefully farmed oysters, and these considerably less expensive cultured pearls subsequently flooded international markets precisely at the historical moment when a worldwide economic depression was simultaneously and sharply reducing overall consumer demand for luxury goods of every conceivable kind. Subsequently, petroleum was discovered within Saudi Arabia in 1938, offering former pearl divers considerably more dependable, safer, and ultimately more lucrative employment opportunities in the emerging industry. Today, traditional pearl diving survives primarily as treasured cultural heritage rather than as an active industry, commemorated extensively in dedicated museums, traditional songs passed down through generations, and regional festivals held throughout the area each year.

MID.prompt: Explain two reasons pearl diving declined in the Gulf and how this changed people's lives.
checklist: I explained the effect of farmed pearls.
I explained the effect of oil.
I used at least two key words.
MID.modelAnswer: Pearl diving declined for two main reasons. First, in Japan people learned to grow cultured pearls on farms, and these cheaper pearls flooded the markets, so natural pearls were worth much less. Second, oil was discovered in Saudi Arabia in 1938, so many men left the sea for jobs in the oil industry instead. This caused a big decline in income for the diving crews, and many families changed their whole way of life.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how both a change in technology and a change in the economy ended the pearling era, and why people still value this heritage today.
checklist: I explained cultured pearls and their effect on prices.
I explained how oil offered new jobs.
I explained how the heritage is remembered.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Both a change in technology and a change in the economy ended the pearling era. In Japan, people discovered how to grow cultured pearls, and because the irritant that forms the pearl's layers of nacre could now be placed inside oysters on farms, these cheaper pearls flooded the market and lowered prices for natural pearls. At the same time, the economy changed when oil was discovered in Saudi Arabia in 1938, giving men a new livelihood in the oil industry instead of risking their lives diving. Even though the industry declined, people still value this heritage today because it represents the courage and skill of the divers who once depended on the sea.
